'''Michael Eugene Nicolas Majerus''' (13 February 1954 – 27 January 2009) was a British [[geneticist]] and professor of evolution at the [[University of Cambridge]]. He was also a teaching fellow at [[Clare College, Cambridge]]. He was an enthusiast in [[Natural selection|Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection]] and became a world authority in his field of insect [[evolutionary biology]]. He was widely noted for his work on [[moth]]s and [[ladybird]]s and as an advocate of the science of [[evolution]]. He was also an enthusiastic educator<ref>For example: {{cite journal | last=Majerus | first=M.E.N. | year=2008 | title=Signs of Darwin in your back garden: The defensive colour patterns of moths and butterflies | journal=AES Bug Club | volume=16 | pages=29–40 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1007/s12052-008-0107-y | last=Majerus | first=M.E.N. | title=Industrial Melanism in the Peppered Moth, ''Biston betularia'': An Excellent Teaching Example of Darwinian Evolution in Action | journal=Evolution: Education and Outreach | volume= 2 | pages=63–74 | year=2009 | doi-access=free }}</ref> and the author of several books on insects,<ref>{{cite book | last=Majerus | first=M. E. N. | year=1994 | title=Ladybirds | publisher=Collins, London, UK | series=New Naturalist series, #81 | isbn=978-0-00-219935-3 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book | last=Majerus | first=M. E. N. | year=2002 | title=Moths | publisher=Collins, London, UK | series=New Naturalist series, #90 | isbn=978-0-00-220142-1 }}</ref> evolution<ref>{{cite book | last1=Majerus | first1=M. E. N. | last2=Amos | first2=W. D. | last3=Hurst | first3=G. D. D. | year=1996 | title=Evolution the Four Billion Year War | publisher=Longman, UK | isbn=978-0-582-21569-6 }}</ref><ref name="melanism1998">{{cite book | last=Majerus | first=M. E. N. | year=1998 | title=Melanism: Evolution in Action | publisher=Oxford University Press, Oxford, UK | isbn=978-0-19-854982-6 }}</ref> and sexual reproduction.<ref>{{cite book | last=Majerus | first=M. E. N. | year=2003 | title=Sex Wars: Genes Bacteria and Biased Sex Ratios | publisher=Princeton University Press, Princeton, USA | isbn=978-0-691-00981-0 }}</ref> He is best remembered as an ardent supporter and champion of experiments on [[peppered moth evolution]].<ref name=bha>{{cite web|title=Professor Michael Majerus (1954–2009)|url=https://humanism.org.uk/about/our-people/distinguished-supporters/michael-majerus/|publisher=British Humanist Association|access-date=24 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Gregory|first1=TR|title=Dr. Michael Majerus (1954–2009)|url=http://www.genomicron.evolverzone.com/2009/01/dr-michael-majerus-1954-2009/|work=Genomicron|date=28 January 2009 |access-date=24 July 2014}}</ref>

== Biography ==

The son of Fernand and Muriel Majerus, Michael Majerus took an early interest in insects. He got his first butterfly net at the age of four. His father, a [[Luxembourg (Belgium)|Luxembourg]] national by origin, encouraged him by taking him for field trips on weekends and bringing him home specimens from his travels.<ref name=clare>{{cite web|title=Professor Michael Majerus (1954–2009)|url=http://www.clarealumni.com/s/845/1col.aspx?sid=845&gid=1&pgid=795|publisher=Clare College|access-date=24 July 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140727042747/http://www.clarealumni.com/s/845/1col.aspx?sid=845&gid=1&pgid=795|archive-date=27 July 2014}}</ref> He was particularly interested in [[lepidoptera]]ns and [[ecological genetics]] following the work of [[E.B. Ford]], whose book ''Moths'' (in the ''[[New Naturalist]]'' series)<ref>{{cite book | last=Ford | first=E.B. | year=1955 | edition=1st | title=Moths | series=New Naturalist #30 | publisher=HarperCollins, London, UK }}</ref> he bought at the age of ten. He was educated at [[Merchant Taylors' School, Northwood]], and graduated in botany and zoology from [[Royal Holloway College]], London. He earned his PhD from Royal Holloway College on the study of the genetic control of larval colour in the [[angle shades]] moth. He worked for two years at [[Keele University]] as a research demonstrator. In 1980 he joined the Department of Genetics at the [[University of Cambridge]] as a research associate. After promotion as lecturer in 1987 and reader in 2001, he was appointed professor of evolution in 2006. In 1990 he was elected fellow of Clare College, and from the next year, in 1991, he became a teaching fellow of the college, the post he held until his death.<ref name=independent>{{cite news|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-michael-majerus-geneticist-who-defended-darwin-in-the-battle-against-creationism-1608181.html |archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/archive/20220514/https://www.independent.co.uk/news/obituaries/professor-michael-majerus-geneticist-who-defended-darwin-in-the-battle-against-creationism-1608181.html |archive-date=14 May 2022 |url-access=subscription |url-status=live|title=Professor Michael Majerus: Geneticist who defended Darwin in the battle against creationism|work=[[The Independent]]|date=13 February 2009|access-date=24 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Reisz|first1=Matthew|title=Obituary: Michael Majerus, 1954-2009|url=http://www.timeshighereducation.co.uk/news/people/obituaries/michael-majerus-1954-2009/405466.article|access-date=24 July 2014|work=Times Higher Education|date=26 February 2009}}</ref>

He died 27 January 2009 after an unexpected and brief struggle with aggressive [[mesothelioma]].

=== Personal life ===

Majerus was a passionate anti-[[creationism|creationist]]. He used much of his scientific works to argue against creationism.<ref name=bha/>

He married Vicki Maclean in 1979, but their marriage was dissolved. He remarried Tamsin Harris in 1988 with whom he had two sons, and one daughter. They later divorced, and Majerus married, for the third time, Christina Poole in 2005.<ref name=independent/>

== Achievements ==

After his doctoral work on moths, Majerus moved into studying ladybirds, an area which brought him widespread publicity as an expert in 2004 when the [[Harmonia axyridis|harlequin ladybird]] came to Britain, causing a [[Invasive species|disaster for native species]]. This publicity led to the involvement of members of the public in the effective monitoring of the spread of the harlequin. His work on the [[peppered moth]] provided new support for the understanding of [[peppered moth evolution]].<ref name="melanism1998"/><ref>{{cite journal | doi=10.1111/j.1365-2311.2008.00987.x | last=Majerus | first=M. E. N. | year=2008 | title=Non-morph specific predation of peppered moths (''Biston betularia'') by bats | journal=Ecological Entomology |volume=33 | pages=679–683 | issue=5 | bibcode=2008EcoEn..33..679M | s2cid=86546684 }}</ref><ref name=deptgen>{{cite web |url=http://www.gen.cam.ac.uk/research/personal/majerus/majerus.html |title=University of Cambridge, Department of Genetics |date=31 March 2010 |work=Professor Mike Majerus 1954–2009 |access-date=2010-08-05 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110615081704/http://www.gen.cam.ac.uk/research/personal/majerus/majerus.html |archive-date=15 June 2011 }}</ref>

=== Peppered moth evolution ===

The legacy of Majerus was largely built on his fervent defence and experimental works on the peppered moth evolution.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Proffitt|first1=F|title=Michael Majerus profile. In defense of Darwin and a former icon of evolution|journal=Science|year=2004|volume=304|issue=5679|pages=1894–5|doi=10.1126/science.304.5679.1894|pmid=15218121|s2cid=33510517}}</ref> The concept of [[industrial melanism]] in ''[[Biston betularia]]'' had been a primary example of Darwinian natural selection in action. With the experimental evidence of [[Bernard Kettlewell]] in the early 1950s, the story became a classic in evolutionary biology. However, the rise of creationism towards the end of 20th century brought forth serious attack. To increase the controversy, biologists also began to argue the validity of [[Kettlewell's experiment]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Majerus|first1=Michael E. N.|title=Industrial Melanism in the Peppered Moth, Biston betularia: An Excellent Teaching Example of Darwinian Evolution in Action|journal=Evolution: Education and Outreach|year=2008|volume=2|issue=1|pages=63–74|doi=10.1007/s12052-008-0107-y|doi-access=free}}</ref> The publication of ''[[Melanism: Evolution in Action]]'' in 1998 in which Majerus analysed and defended Kettlewell's experiments provoked severe criticism. Kettlewell's works were seen as lacking proper experimental procedure, with some even accusing it variously as a fake, fraudulent, hoax and wrong.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Miller|first1=Ken|title=The Peppered Moth – An Update|url=http://www.millerandlevine.com/km/evol/Moths/moths.html|website=millerandlevine.com|access-date=25 July 2014|year=1999}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Peppered Moth|url=http://www.truthinscience.org.uk/tis2/index.php/evidence-for-evolution-mainmenu-65/127-the-peppered-moth.html|work=truthinscience|publisher=Truth in Science|access-date=25 July 2014|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140812195432/http://www.truthinscience.org.uk/tis2/index.php/evidence-for-evolution-mainmenu-65/127-the-peppered-moth.html|archive-date=12 August 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last1=Grant|first1=Bruce|title=Charges of fraud misleading|url=http://www.millerandlevine.com/km/evol/Moths/grant-pratt-tribune.html|work=The Pratt Tribune|access-date=25 July 2014|date=13 December 2000}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cook|first1=Laurence M.|title=The Rise and Fall of the Form of the Peppered Moth|journal=The Quarterly Review of Biology|year=2003|volume=78|issue=4|pages=399–417|doi=10.1086/378925|pmid=14737825|s2cid=26831926}}</ref> The accusations were most influentially popularised by [[Judith Hooper]] in her 2002 book ''[[Of Moths and Men]]'' (which in turn received severe criticisms).<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Grant|first1=B. S|title=Sour Grapes of Wrath|journal=Science|year=2002|volume=297|issue=5583|pages=940–941|doi=10.1126/science.1073593|s2cid=161367302}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Clarke|first1=Bryan|title=The art of innuendo|journal=Heredity|year=2003|volume=90|issue=4|pages=279–280|doi=10.1038/sj.hdy.6800229|doi-access=free}}</ref> One of the critics, [[Jerry Coyne]], himself a professor of evolution at the [[University of Chicago]], commented that: "[M]ost of the work described is inconclusive... for the time being we must discard ''Biston'' as a well-understood example of natural selection in action, although it is clearly a case of evolution."<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Coyne|first1=Jerry A|title=Not black and white|journal=Nature|year=1998|volume=396|issue=1|pages=35–36|doi=10.1038/23856|bibcode=1998Natur.396...35C|doi-access=free}}</ref> Majerus then designed an elaborate experiment to resolve the issues.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Majerus|first1=Michael EN|title=Non-morph specific predation of peppered moths (''Biston betularia'') by bats|journal=Ecological Entomology|year=2008|volume=33|issue=5|pages=679–683|doi=10.1111/j.1365-2311.2008.00987.x|bibcode=2008EcoEn..33..679M |s2cid=86546684}}</ref> Starting from 2001 he conducted experiments for seven years, and terminated by his own death. He had experimented with 4,864 moths in Cambridgeshire, becoming the largest experiment in such manner. After his death his experimental results were analysed by a collaboration of American and British geneticists, and was published in 2012.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Luiggi|first1=Cristina|title=Mighty Moth Man|journal=The Scientists|date=1 May 2012|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/32032/title/Mighty-Moth-Man/|access-date=25 July 2014}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Cook|first1=L. M.|last2=Grant|first2=B. S.|last3=Saccheri|first3=I. J.|last4=Mallet|first4=J.|title=Selective bird predation on the peppered moth: the last experiment of Michael Majerus|journal=Biology Letters|year=2012|volume=8|issue=4|pages=609–612|doi=10.1098/rsbl.2011.1136|pmid=22319093|pmc=3391436}}</ref> Majerus's works clearly vindicated the experiments on peppered moth evolution, and the paper concluded that:
{{blockquote|The new data, coupled with the weight of previously existing data convincingly show that 'industrial melanism in the peppered moth is still one of the clearest and most easily understood examples of Darwinian evolution in action'.}}

== Honours and recognitions ==

Majerus was the president of the [[Amateur Entomologists' Society]],<ref>{{cite journal | last=Majerus | first=M.E.N. | year=2008 | title=Natural history and the future of the world: Presidential Address given at the Amateur Entomologists' Society AGM on 26th April 2008 | journal=Bulletin of the Amateur Entomologists' Society | volume=67 | pages=89–98 }}</ref> a Fellow of the [[Royal Entomological Society]], and a Life Fellow of the [[British Naturalists' Association]]. He received a number of awards, including the [[British Naturalists' Association#Peter Scott Memorial Award|Peter Scott Memorial Award]] in 2006, for his contributions to British [[Natural History]]. In 2004 he was conferred the title "Distinguished Supporter" of the [[British Humanist Association]].<ref name=bha/> In 2010 the 
Amateur Entomologists' Society launched ''The Mike Majerus Grant'' with the aim of encouraging a new generation of entomologists by supporting and funding projects based in the British Isles which further the cause of entomological study, research or education by amateurs, especially the young.
<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.amentsoc.org/about/majerus-grant.html |title=The Michael Majerus Grant |access-date=2015-08-24}}</ref>
